abstract: Copy number variants (CNVs) are prevalent in both diploid and haploid genomes and contribute to genome evolution and phenotypic diversity. However, CNV detection in low-input data, including low-cell and single-cell sequencing data, remains challenging due to the shallow and highly uneven read counts and amplification bias. Another challenge lies in selecting reference samples, which are used to provide a baseline for defining copy-number losses or gains. Normalization using references containing common CNVs can lead to cancellation of true CNV signals or false CNV calls. Here, we develop GapCNV, a statistical framework for CNV detection in low-input DNA sequencing data from both haploid and diploid genomes. GapCNV uses preliminary cell clustering and shared CNV profiles to construct bin-specific pseudo-references from cells inferred to have the copy-neutral state. This strategy reduces the incorporation of common CNVs into the normalization baseline and thereby preserves common CNV signals. We evaluated GapCNV using simulations with and without amplification biases and datasets from Plasmodium falciparum, human breast cancer and melanoma. In simulations, GapCNV achieved high precision rate while maintaining competitive sensitivity, with advantages for detecting short and common CNVs. In P. falciparum, GapCNV detected the known CNVs and recovered the short CNV more frequently than the benchmarking methods. In the melanoma cell line and human breast tumors, GapCNV recovered bulk or single-cell derived copy number profile across individual cells. These results show that adaptive, bin-specific pseudo-reference construction can improve CNV detection when reliable normal controls are unavailable.
